## Key finding: your assumptions about this repo don't hold

I searched the entire repository and there is **no `pkg/rules/` directory**, no file named or resembling `workload-privileged-hostpath-escape.yaml`, no `pkg/rules/*_test.go` files, and no custom CEL function/macro like `getPodSpec` in `pkg/engine`. This repo (module `github.com/madhuakula/spotter`, at `D:\gsb-auto\batches\pointwise-20261109\019-spotter\A`) is a **CLI/engine-only snapshot** of the Spotter project. The actual rule content (hundreds of YAML rules) lives externally on the Spotter Hub (`rules.spotter.dev` / `rules.spotter.run`) and is fetched over HTTP at runtime via `pkg/hub/client.go`, optionally cached to a configurable local directory (not `pkg/rules/`).

Below is everything that does exist, which is what you'll actually be working against.

### 1. Directory structure / schema — only two template files exist, under `misc/`

No `pkg/rules/` subdirectories by security category exist in the repo tree. `pkg/models/rule.go` does define category *constants* (used only for documentation/labels), not directories:
`Workload Security`, `Access Control`, `Network & Traffic Security`, `Secrets & Data Protection`, `Configuration & Resource Hygiene`, `Supply Chain & Image Security`, `Audit, Logging & Compliance`, `Platform & Infrastructure Security`.

The only rule-shaped YAML in the repo is `D:\gsb-auto\batches\pointwise-20261109\019-spotter\A\misc\example-rule-strucutre.yaml` (full content reproduced above — note the typo "strucutre" in the actual filename). This is the canonical schema reference and is explicitly a privileged-container-detection example. Its structure:

```yaml
apiVersion: rules.spotter.dev/v1alpha1
kind: SpotterRule
metadata:
  name: spotter-<category>-<nnn>        # e.g. spotter-workload-001
  labels:
    severity: "high"                    # low|medium|high|critical
    category: "workload"                # workload|access|config|data|network|platform|supply|audit
  annotations:
    rules.spotter.dev/title: "..."
    rules.spotter.dev/version: "1.0.0"
    rules.spotter.dev/description: "..."
    rules.spotter.dev/cwe: "CWE-269"    # optional
    rules.spotter.dev/author: "..."     # optional
spec:
  match:
    resources:
      kubernetes:
        apiGroups: ["", "apps", "batch"]
        versions: ["v1", "v1beta1"]
        kinds: ["Pod","Deployment","StatefulSet","DaemonSet","Job","CronJob"]
        namespaces:
          include: ["*"]
          exclude: ["kube-system", "kube-public", "kube-node-lease"]
        labels:
          include: { environment: ["production","staging"] }
          exclude: { rules.spotter.dev/ignore: ["true"] }
  cel: |
    <CEL expression, must evaluate to boolean true = VIOLATION FOUND>
  remediation:
    manual: |
      <free text, markdown fenced examples ok>
    # auto:
    #   patch:
    #     - op: "replace"
    #       path: "/spec/containers/0/securityContext/privileged"
    #       value: false
  references:
    - title: "..."
      url: "..."
```

There is a second template, `misc/example-rule-pack-structure.yaml`, showing a `SpotterRulePack` (`kind: SpotterRulePack`) that just lists rule IDs plus `references`.

### 2. Multi-kind CEL pattern — no generic pod-spec helper exists

There is **no CEL macro/function that normalizes podSpec across kinds**. The one example rule handles the Pod-vs-workload path split by hand inside the CEL expression itself, using `object.kind` branching:

```yaml
cel: |
  (object.kind == 'Pod' && (
    (has(object.spec.containers) &&
     object.spec.containers.exists(c,
       has(c.securityContext) &&
       has(c.securityContext.privileged) &&
       c.securityContext.privileged == true)) ||
    (has(object.spec.initContainers) &&
     object.spec.initContainers.exists(c,
       has(c.securityContext) &&
       has(c.securityContext.privileged) &&
       c.securityContext.privileged == true))
  )) || (object.kind != 'Pod' && (
    (has(object.spec.template.spec.containers) &&
     object.spec.template.spec.containers.exists(c,
       has(c.securityContext) &&
       has(c.securityContext.privileged) &&
       c.securityContext.privileged == true)) ||
    (has(object.spec.template.spec.initContainers) &&
     object.spec.template.spec.initContainers.exists(c,
       has(c.securityContext) &&
       has(c.securityContext.privileged) &&
       c.securityContext.privileged == true))
  ))
```

Note this pattern does **not** cover CronJob's extra `jobTemplate.spec.template.spec` nesting — it only handles `object.spec` (Pod) vs `object.spec.template.spec` (Deployment/StatefulSet/DaemonSet/Job). If your new rule needs to also match CronJob, you must add a third branch for `object.spec.jobTemplate.spec.template.spec`, following the same hand-rolled `||` pattern — there's no existing helper to reuse, no `cel.Macro` registration, and no "generic pod extractor" anywhere in `pkg/engine`.

There are no additional multi-kind example rule files beyond this single one — I could not find 2–3 more as hoped, because there is exactly one example rule file in the whole repository.

### CEL environment setup — `pkg/engine/cel.go`

`NewCELEngine()` (`D:\gsb-auto\batches\pointwise-20261109\019-spotter\A\pkg\engine\cel.go` lines 26–102) builds the `cel.Env` with:
- Variables: `object` (`cel.DynType`), `oldObject`, `request`, `authorizer` (`DynType`), `namespace` (`StringType`), `cluster` (`DynType`)
- Standard extensions: `ext.Strings()`, `ext.Encoders()`, `ext.Math()`, `ext.Lists()`, `ext.Sets()`
- Custom functions registered via `cel.Function(...)`: `hasLabel(string)`, `hasAnnotation(string)`, `isSystemNamespace(string)`, `hasSecurityContext(dyn)` — **but `hasLabel`, `hasAnnotation`, and `hasSecurityContext` are stub placeholders that always return `true`** (see comments "Placeholder" at lines 50, 58, 78). Only `isSystemNamespace` is actually implemented. Do not rely on `hasLabel`/`hasAnnotation`/`hasSecurityContext` in new rules — they're broken stubs in this codebase snapshot.
- No `cel.Macro(...)` calls anywhere in the repo (`grep -r "cel.Macro"` returns nothing).
- `cel.HomogeneousAggregateLiterals()`, `cel.EagerlyValidateDeclarations(true)`, `cel.DefaultUTCTimeZone(true)`, `cel.OptionalTypes()`.

`EvaluateRule` (lines 203–278) is how `object` is passed into the activation:
```go
vars := map[string]interface{}{
    "object":     resource,   // resource is map[string]interface{} — raw unstructured JSON/YAML
    "oldObject":  nil,
    "request":    nil,
    "authorizer": nil,
}
eval, _, err := celProgram.Eval(vars)
```
The CEL boolean convention is inverted from "pass": **`true` return = violation found**. The engine does `result.Passed = !boolResult`.

A second, separate, smaller CEL lib exists in `pkg/testing/runner.go` (`kubernetesLib`) used only by the test harness, registering `has_label`, `get_label`, `has_annotation`, `get_annotation` as **binary** functions `(object, key)` — different naming/signature convention than the ones in `pkg/engine/cel.go`. These two CEL environments are not unified; be aware a rule written using `hasLabel("x")` (unary, engine style) will not compile under the test runner's environment, and vice versa for `has_label(object, "x")`. Since both are placeholders or inconsistent, **don't use either** — just write plain CEL using `has()`/`exists()`/`object.metadata.labels[...]` directly, which is what the one real example does.

### 3. Loader — `pkg/parser/loader.go`

File discovery: `LoadFromDirectory(dirPath)` (`D:\gsb-auto\batches\pointwise-20261109\019-spotter\A\pkg\parser\loader.go` lines 96–137) walks a directory recursively via `filepath.Walk`, picks up any file ending in `.yaml` or `.yml`, and **skips** any path containing `-test.` or `_test.` (reserved for test-case files, see point 4). There's no enforced filename-to-id convention in the loader itself — the hub client's cache writer (`pkg/hub/client.go` `SaveRuleToCache`, line ~239) does write files as `<rule-id>.yaml`, but the parser doesn't require that; it keys everything off the YAML `kind:` field, not the filename.

Parsing: `LoadFromBytes` splits on `\n---\n` for multi-doc files, peeks `kind:` via a tiny anonymous struct, then dispatches to `parseSpotterRule` or `parseSpotterRulePack`, both of which just do `yaml.Unmarshal` into the Go structs in `pkg/models/rule.go`. **There is no JSON Schema** — validation is pure Go code in `pkg/validation/validator.go`.

Schema validation (`ValidateSpotterRule`, `D:\gsb-auto\batches\pointwise-20261109\019-spotter\A\pkg\validation\validator.go` lines 29–142) enforces, in order:
- `apiVersion == "rules.spotter.dev/v1alpha1"` exactly
- `kind == "SpotterRule"` exactly
- `metadata.name` required and must match regex `^spotter-[a-z]+(-[a-z]+)*-\d{3}$` (lowercase, hyphenated category, exactly 3 digits — e.g. `spotter-workload-001`; `spotter-workload-01` or `-0001` both fail)
- `metadata.annotations` required, with required keys `rules.spotter.dev/title`, `rules.spotter.dev/version`, `rules.spotter.dev/description`
- `metadata.labels` required, with required keys `severity` (must be one of `low|medium|high|critical`) and `category` (any non-empty string)
- `spec.cel` required and must compile + type-check to `cel.BoolType` under a throwaway env (`object`, `oldObject`, `request` as `DynType`)
- `spec.match.resources.kubernetes.kinds` must have at least one entry

No registry/index file needs updating — there's no central rule list in Go code; discovery is purely directory-walk-based at runtime (or hub-fetch-based).

### 4. Test harness

There are **no `_test.go` files under any rules package** (none exists) and no individual rule YAML test fixtures in the repo. What exists instead:

**a) `pkg/testing/runner.go`** — a generic harness designed to run a rule's `RuleTestSuite` (a YAML-declared list of test cases, not Go tests). Relevant model (`pkg/models/rule.go` lines 347–355):
```go
type RuleTestCase struct {
    Name  string `yaml:"name" json:"name"`
    Pass  bool   `yaml:"pass" json:"pass"`     // true = should NOT violate
    Input string `yaml:"input" json:"input"`   // raw YAML of a k8s object, as a string
}
type RuleTestSuite []RuleTestCase
```
`parser.LoadTestCases(testFilePath)` and `parser.GetRuleTestFile(ruleFilePath)` (loader.go lines 182–203) show the convention: for a rule file `foo.yaml`, its test file is expected at `foo-test.yaml` in the same directory (hence the loader's directory walk skipping `-test.`/`_test.` substrings).

`RuleTestRunner.RunTestSuite` (runner.go lines 60–96): compiles `rule.Spec.CEL` once via its own `cel.Env` (imports `cel`, `types`, `ref` from `cel-go`, plus `gopkg.in/yaml.v3`, `pkg/models`, `pkg/validation`), then for each test case unmarshals `testCase.Input` YAML into `map[string]interface{}`, evaluates with `vars := map[string]interface{}{"object": kubernetesObject}`, and checks `boolVal == !testCase.Pass` (violation-found convention, same inversion as the engine).

**b) `pkg/validation/validator_test.go`** — standard Go `*_test.go` using table-driven tests, constructing `*models.SpotterRule` literals directly in Go (not via YAML parsing) and calling `validation.ValidateSpotterRule(rule)` / `ValidateSpotterRulePack` / `validateCELExpression` / `isValidRuleName` / `isValidRulePackName`, asserting on `.Valid` and error message substrings. This is the pattern to follow if you write Go unit tests for a new rule's validity, but it does not exercise the CEL-against-a-k8s-object evaluation path (that's `pkg/testing/runner.go`'s job, driven by YAML test-suite files, not Go tests).

If you want an end-to-end Go test for your new rule's CEL logic, the realistic pattern (synthesized from what exists, since no rule-specific `_test.go` exists to copy) is:
```go
import (
    "github.com/madhuakula/spotter/pkg/models"
    "github.com/madhuakula/spotter/pkg/testing"
)
rule := &models.SpotterRule{ /* ... */ Spec: models.RuleSpec{CEL: "..."} }
suite := models.RuleTestSuite{
    {Name: "privileged pod violates", Pass: false, Input: podYAMLString},
    {Name: "non-privileged pod ok", Pass: true, Input: safePodYAMLString},
}
runner, _ := testing.NewRuleTestRunner()
result, _ := runner.RunTestSuite(rule, suite)
```

### 5. Privileged / capabilities detection patterns

The only real example (`misc/example-rule-strucutre.yaml`) checks exactly:
```
has(c.securityContext) && has(c.securityContext.privileged) && c.securityContext.privileged == true
```
applied via `.exists(c, ...)` separately to `object.spec.containers` and `object.spec.initContainers`, each guarded by `has(object.spec.containers)` / `has(object.spec.initContainers)`, joined with `||`. It does **not** combine the two lists with `+` concatenation — it writes the `.exists()` twice, once per list, OR'd together. There is no existing example checking capabilities like `SYS_ADMIN` anywhere in the repo (`grep -ri "SYS_ADMIN\|capabilities" pkg/ misc/` turns up nothing beyond this). The `validator_test.go` fixture (line 44) uses a simpler single-list variant for Pod-only matching:
```
object.spec.containers.exists(c, has(c.securityContext) && has(c.securityContext.privileged) && c.securityContext.privileged == true)
```

If you want to combine containers + initContainers into one `.exists()` call (list concatenation with `+`) for a hostPath-style rule, that's a pattern you'd be introducing fresh — nothing in this codebase currently does it, so there's no convention to match beyond "guard with `has()` before dereferencing, use `.exists(c, ...)` for OR-semantics across a container list."

### 6. go.mod / build

`D:\gsb-auto\batches\pointwise-20261109\019-spotter\A\go.mod`: module `github.com/madhuakula/spotter`, `go 1.24.0`, toolchain `go1.24.5`. Key deps: `github.com/google/cel-go v0.26.0`, `k8s.io/api`, `k8s.io/apimachinery`, `k8s.io/client-go v0.33.3`, `gopkg.in/yaml.v3`, `sigs.k8s.io/yaml`.

`Makefile` targets (`D:\gsb-auto\batches\pointwise-20261109\019-spotter\A\Makefile`): `make build` (plain `go build`), `make test` → `go test -v -race -coverprofile=coverage.out ./...`, `make test-coverage`, `make lint` → `golangci-lint run ./...`, `make fmt` → `go fmt ./...`, `make vet` → `go vet ./...`, `make check` → `fmt vet lint test` combined. **No `.github/workflows` directory exists** in this snapshot, so there's no CI YAML to consult for additional standards beyond the Makefile.

### Bottom line for writing your rule

Since `pkg/rules/` doesn't exist, you have a decision to make before writing code: either (a) create a new `pkg/rules/` tree yourself (no precedent dictates its internal layout — you'd be establishing the category-subdirectory convention from scratch, using the `SecurityCategory` constants in `pkg/models/rule.go` as your category names), or (b) place the new rule wherever the actual deployment expects local rules to be loaded from (check `pkg/config` for `RulesDir`/`PacksDir` defaults — `pkg/config/loader.go` references `config.RulesDir`/`config.PacksDir` but I did not locate the default path values in `pkg/config/config.go` during this pass; worth confirming before deciding on a location). Either way, the YAML schema to follow is the one in `misc/example-rule-strucutre.yaml` reproduced in full above, validated against `pkg/validation/validator.go`'s rules, loadable via `pkg/parser/loader.go`, and evaluated via `pkg/engine/cel.go`'s `object`-keyed CEL activation with the "CEL true = violation" convention.

        # List all resource types that this security rule should evaluate

          - "StatefulSet"   # Stateful workloads
          - "DaemonSet"     # Node-level workloads
          - "Job"           # Batch jobs

  # This expression evaluates to true when a security violation is detected
  # The 'object' variable contains the Kubernetes resource being evaluated
  cel: |
    // Check for privileged containers in both Pods and workload resources
    // This rule detects containers running with privileged security context
    
    (object.kind == 'Pod' && (
      // For direct Pod resources, check containers and initContainers
      (has(object.spec.containers) && 
       object.spec.containers.exists(c, 
         has(c.securityContext) && 
         has(c.securityContext.privileged) && 
         c.securityContext.privileged == true)) ||

         has(c.securityContext.privileged) &&

    manual: |
